Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Our analysis introduces a subspace virtual iterate to resolve the coupling between the momentum and the residual correction. Furthermore, we extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant which periodically recomputes bases to track the evolving dominant subspace and retains the same rate. Since each basis refresh breaks the consistency of the virtual iterates, we devise a boundary correction approach that aligns them across stages. Beyond momentum SGD, we incorporate our framework into Muon and propose PMRC, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. Through a weighted momentum tracking analysis that accounts for the residual gradient, we establish an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate for PMRC, which matches the rate of full-space Muon. We also design a multi-stage PMRC with periodically refreshed bases, which maintains a convergence rate of the same order. Extensive experimental results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms.

Large language models (LLMs) ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; OpenAI, 2023 ; Bai et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) have demonstrated strong capabilities in dialogue ( Thoppilan et al., 2022 ) , language understanding ( Chowdhery et al., 2023 ) , mathematical reasoning ( Lewkowycz et al., 2022 ) and code generation ( Chen et al., 2021 ) . As model scale grows, training imposes substantial computational and memory demands ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Chowdhery et al., 2023 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ) . The widely used AdamW optimizer ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) further increases memory consumption, since its first- and second-moment estimates are each as large as the model itself. To alleviate the memory overhead, recent work has explored different forms of memory-efficient training, ranging from restricting the set of trainable parameters ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Ben Zaken et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) to maintaining optimizer states in low-dimensional subspaces ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Pan et al., 2025a ) . In this work, we focus on memory-efficient subspace optimization, which reduces optimization memory by maintaining the optimizer states in a low-dimensional subspace. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) is a representative method in this line of work. For a weight matrix W t ∈ ℝ m × n W_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , GaLore utilizes an orthonormal basis P ∈ ℝ m × r P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} with r ≪ min ⁡ { m , n } r\ll\min\{m,n\} and projects the gradient G t ∈ ℝ m × n G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} into the space ℝ r × n \mathbb{R}^{r\times n} , where the optimizer maintains its states, reducing the memory complexity from O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn)

gradient G t ∈ ℝ m × n G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} into the space ℝ r × n \mathbb{R}^{r\times n} , where the optimizer maintains its states, reducing the memory complexity from O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) to O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . To construct the projection matrix, GaLore computes the leading singular vectors of the stochastic gradient to capture its dominant directions and periodically recomputes P P via SVD during training.

As shown by He et al. (2025) , GaLore may fail to converge to a stationary point under standard stochastic assumptions. Since the projection basis is estimated from stochastic gradients, whose leading singular directions can be dominated by anisotropic noise rather than the true gradient in later training stages, the selected subspace fails to capture gradient directions. While GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) replaces the SVD basis with random projections and establishes convergence under standard assumptions, its random subspaces do not exploit dominant gradient directions and are less effective in practice. Recent methods that retain gradient-dependent subspaces either require stronger assumptions ( Robert et al., 2025 ) or offer no memory advantage in the worst case ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . Therefore, there still remains a lack of convergence guarantees for memory-efficient subspace optimization with gradient-dependent dominant subspaces under standard assumptions.

Subspace Momentum SGD with Residual Correction (SMRC). Inspired by Chen et al. (2025a) , we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains optimizer states in a low-dimensional subspace and adds the residual gradient in its orthogonal complement to the update. We incorporate this framework into momentum SGD ( Liu et al., 2020 ) and propose SMRC, which keeps momentum only in the projected space and reduces optimizer-state memory from O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) to O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . Although the projected momentum update and the residual correction lie in orthogonal subspaces, they remain coupled across iterations. To overcome this difficulty, we devise a subspace virtual iterate strategy that absorbs the momentum into an auxiliary trajectory. SMRC achieves an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate for any fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Furthermore, since the dominant gradient subspace evolves during training, practical methods periodically refresh the projection matrix P P , and we accordingly extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant. A direct application of the single-stage analysis results in a mismatch between virtual iterates at stage boundaries. We design a boundary correction approach that preserves the consistency of the virtual sequence. Our multi-stage SMRC attains the same rate as that of single-stage SMRC.

Projected Muon with Residual Correction (PMRC). Beyond momentum SGD, we apply the residual correction framework to Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , an effective optimizer for LLM training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , and develop PMRC. It maintains momentum in the projected coordinates and applies the matrix sign to the low-dimensional momentum. This nonlinear dependence of the update on the momentum invalidates the subspace virtual-iterate construction used for SMRC. To address this challenge, we present a weighted momentum tracking analysis that jointly characterizes momentum accumulation and effects induced by the residual correction. The matrix-sign step corresponds to steepest descent under the spectral norm and is characterized by the nuclear norm ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) , whereas the residual gradient correction is measured in the Frobenius norm. We establish convergence under a mixed stationarity measure and PMRC attains the same O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) rate as that of full-space Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . Similarly, we generalize PMRC to a multi-stage setting with periodically refreshed projection bases that better capture the evolving dominant gradient subspace and improve practical performance. The multi-stage variant retains the same O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate.

Finally, we evaluate our methods through extensive experiments. On synthetic problems, we examine the residual correction and the multi-stage basis refresh in SMRC, and the results show that the residual correction restores convergence while periodic refreshes track the evolving dominant gradient subspace. For practical LLM training, we develop a practical implementation of PMRC and evaluate it on LLaMA pretraining across four model scales from 60 60 M to 1.3 1.3 B parameters and on six supervised finetuning settings. Our PMRC consistently performs favorably against prior memory-efficient methods across different model scales and training settings.
In this section, we briefly review related work on memory-efficient optimization and on Muon and its variants. Due to space limitations, we provide additional discussion in Appendix A .

As model scale grows, full-parameter training becomes increasingly memory-intensive, since gradients and optimizer states impose substantial overhead. Parameter-efficient finetuning methods reduce this cost by restricting the update to a small set of parameters. LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) freezes the model weights and learns low-rank updates, which is effective for finetuning but limits the expressiveness of the update in pretraining ( Ding et al., 2023 ; Lialin et al., 2024 ) . GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) instead reduces memory by maintaining optimizer states in a low-dimensional gradient subspace. Given a stochastic gradient G t ∈ ℝ m × n G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , where we assume m ≤ n m\leq n without loss of generality, GaLore uses an orthonormal basis P t ∈ ℝ m × r P_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} with r ≪ m r\ll m to form the projected gradient P t ⊤ ​ G t ∈ ℝ r × n P_{t}^{\top}G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} . The optimizer states are maintained in the reduced coordinates and the resulting update is mapped back to the original parameter space through P t P_{t} . GaLore constructs P t P_{t} from the top- r r left singular vectors of the stochastic gradient. Since computing the top- r r SVD at every iteration is expensive, GaLore refreshes P t P_{t} once every τ \tau iterations while keeping it fixed between consecutive refreshes. As shown by He et al. (2025) , the leading singular subspaces computed from stochastic gradients can be dominated by anisotropic noise rather than the true gradient, leaving informative gradient directions outside span ⁡ ( P t ) \mathrm{span}(P_{t}) and preventing convergence under standard stochastic assumptions.

To address this limitation, GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) replaces the SVD basis with random projections. While GoLore establishes convergence guarantees under standard stochastic assumptions, its random subspaces do not preferentially capture dominant gradient directions and lead to slow convergence. Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) follows a complementary approach by retaining the SVD-based subspace and augmenting the projected update with a norm-scaled correction of the discarded residual gradient. Although Fira performs well empirically, its residual scaling is primarily motivated by empirical observations and lacks a convergence guarantee. Zmushko et al. (2025) and Nguyen and Nguyen (2025) also maintain optimizer states in a subspace and apply an SGD-type update in the orthogonal complement. The analysis in Zmushko et al. (2025) is developed for momentum SGD on selected coordinates combined with SGD on the remaining ones. Its convergence guarantee therefore does not directly cover the periodically refreshed SVD subspaces used in GaLore. The convergence rate of Nguyen and Nguyen (2025) is established for a fixed basis under stronger assumptions and applies only to an unweighted residual update.

Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) has demonstrated strong empirical performance in LLM training, outperforming AdamW while exhibiting stable scaling behavior ( Team et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . For matrix-shaped parameters, Muon updates along the matrix sign of the momentum, the steepest-descent direction under the spectral norm, and approximates it efficiently through Newton–Schulz iterations. Despite these advantages, Muon still requires a momentum of the same size as the parameter matrix and incurs the same O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) optimizer-state memory cost as momentum SGD. In recent years, a growing body of work has developed Muon variants to improve its memory efficiency ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Refael et al., 2025 ; Pan et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Anson et al., 2026 ) , and we provide a detailed discussion of these methods in Appendix A.3 . Among them, GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) combines GaLore-style low-rank projection with layerwise sampling. At each sampling period, a subset of layers receives compensated full-rank updates, while the remaining layers receive projected low-rank ones. The two branches are reweighted according to their sampling probabilities. Since the full-rank branches are drawn independently across layers, all layers may be selected at the same time, in which case GUM offers no memory reduction over Muon.

We first present the single-stage SMRC with a fixed orthonormal basis and establish its convergence guarantee. Building on this result, we then propose a multi-stage variant with periodically refreshed bases and show that it retains the same convergence rate.

As discussed above, GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) discards the gradient component outside the subspace, which can prevent convergence under stochastic noise. GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) restores the convergence guarantee through random projections, yet its gradient-independent projection strategy leads to worse practical performance than GaLore. To resolve this dilemma, we adopt a residual correction framework inspired by Chen et al. Although the single-stage analysis accommodates any fixed orthonormal basis P P , practical subspace methods ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2025a ) typically construct P P from the dominant singular subspace of the stochastic gradient so that the projected update retains informative gradient directions. Since the dominant singular subspace of the gradient varies throughout optimization, practical subspace methods periodically update the projection basis to capture the evolving geometry of the loss landscape. Following the periodic refresh strategy of GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , we propose the multi-stage SMRC as presented in Algorithm 2 . It partitions the total N N iterations into K K stages, where stage k k contains T k T_{k} iterations and N = ∑ k = 1 K T k N=\sum_{k=1}^{K}T_{k} . Within each stage k k , SMRC performs T k T_{k} updates using a fixed orthonormal basis P k P_{k} and maintains the corresponding low-dimensional momentum 𝐦 k , t {\mathbf{m}}_{k,t} . At the end of stage k k , a new basis P k + 1 P_{k+1} is computed from the dominant subspace of the stochastic gradient and the subsequent stage proceeds in the refreshed subspace.

The extension of the single-stage analysis to periodically refreshed bases introduces an additional challenge at stage boundaries. If each new stage is initialized with the terminal iterate of the preceding stage, the corresponding virtual sequence becomes inconsistent across basis refreshes. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a boundary correction approach that modifies the iterate at each stage transition to compensate for the offset. The corrected transition ensures the terminal virtual iterate of the stage coincides with the initial virtual iterate of the next. The corresponding convergence guarantee of multi-stage SMRC is stated below.

Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) has demonstrated strong performance in LLM training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , while its full-dimensional momentum incurs the same O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) optimizer-state memory cost as momentum SGD. At larger model scales, this memory requirement becomes increasingly restrictive and motivates the development of memory-efficient variants of Muon ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . A natural question is whether the momentum of Muon can be maintained in a low-dimensional subspace while preserving the convergence guarantee of full-space Muon . We incorporate the residual correction framework into Muon and develop PMRC, as outlined in Algorithm 3 . Specifically, PMRC projects the stochastic gradient G t G_{t} onto the subspace, maintains the low-rank momentum M t = ( 1 − β ) ​ M t − 1 + β ​ P ⊤ ​ G t ∈ ℝ r × n M_{t}=(1-\beta)M_{t-1}+\beta P^{\top}G_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and applies the matrix sign to M t M_{t} . Then, PMRC incorporates the orthogonal residual gradient into the parameter update, that is, W t + 1 = W t − η ⁡ ( P ​ msign ⁡ ( M t ) + γ ⁡ ( I − P ​ P ⊤ ) ​ G t ) W_{t+1}=W_{t}-\eta(P\operatorname{msign}(M_{t})+\gamma(I-PP^{\top})G_{t}) , where γ > 0 \gamma>0 controls the residual correction.

Notably, PMRC combines the Muon update with residual correction and the two update terms are characterized by different norm geometries. The matrix-sign step corresponds to steepest descent under the spectral norm and is characterized by the nuclear norm ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ; Li and Hong, 2025 ) , whereas the residual gradient correction is measured in the Frobenius norm. We analyze PMRC through a weighted momentum-tracking argument for the bias-corrected projected momentum, which accounts for both momentum accumulation and the iterate variation induced by residual correction. In this section, we assess the performance of the proposed methods through LLM pretraining and finetuning tasks. In experiments, we adopt a practical PMRC variant that applies a residual cap to improve training stability and refreshes the basis through an efficient approximation of SVD, as detailed in Appendix E.2.1 . We adopt the LLaMA architecture ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) and train models with 60 60 M, 150 150 M, 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B parameters. Their architectural configurations are summarized in Table 4 . All models are pretrained on the C4 dataset ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) .

Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. In this paper, we investigate memory-efficient subspace optimization and adopt a residual correction framework. For momentum SGD, our proposed SMRC combines projected momentum with a gradient correction in the orthogonal complement and achieves an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate, which matches that of full-space momentum SGD. We generalize SMRC to a multi-stage variant with arbitrary basis refreshes and introduce a boundary correction that aligns consecutive virtual iterates, while retaining a convergence rate of the same order as the single-stage method. Furthermore, we extend this framework to Muon and propose PMRC, which achieves an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) rate under a mixed stationarity measure, while the multi-stage variant retains a convergence rate of the same order. The convergence rates of both PMRC variants are of the same order as that of full-space Muon. Both SMRC and PMRC reduce the optimizer-state memory from O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) to O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . Extensive experimental results on LLM pretraining and supervised finetuning tasks demonstrate the practical effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed methods.

Several methods reduce memory cost through structured restrictions on the trainable parameters. Han et al. (2024) combine sparse and low-rank trainable components to increase the expressiveness of memory-efficient updates. LISA ( Pan et al., 2024 ) periodically resamples a subset of intermediate layers and updates parameters within the selected layers. Another line of work improves the construction and evolution of low-dimensional optimization subspaces. Flora ( Hao et al., 2024 ) repeatedly resamples random low-rank projections, allowing updates from different subspaces to accumulate into higher-rank parameter changes. Muhamed et al. (2024) construct sparse projection matrices from gradient row norms, which reduces the computational cost relative to GaLore. Liang et al. (2024) instead maintain the projection basis through online subspace estimation. SARA ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) samples singular directions according to their importance rather than deterministically retaining only the leading directions. Chen et al. (2025b) formulate training over sampled low-dimensional parameter subspaces, reducing optimizer-state and activation memory.

Comparison with Nguyen and Nguyen (2025) . Nguyen and Nguyen (2025) combine projected momentum with an SGD update in the orthogonal complement. Their convergence guarantee is established for a fixed projection under stronger assumptions, with the residual update restricted to unit weight. It does not provide guarantees for subspace switching or the matrix-sign updates used by Muon. We address these limitations by analyzing weighted residual correction, establishing convergence for multi-stage SMRC with boundary correction, and developing a mixed-geometry analysis for PMRC. Moreover, the proof of Lemma D.1 in Nguyen and Nguyen (2025) contains an error. Other methods reduce memory by directly compressing the optimizer states. Adam-mini ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) replaces elementwise second-moment estimates with a scalar estimate shared within each Hessian-informed parameter block, while retaining the full first-moment estimate. APOLLO ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) estimates channel-wise gradient scaling from low-rank first- and second-moment states constructed using random projections.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) is an efficient finetuning method for LLMs. LoRA reduces the memory cost of finetuning by freezing the pretrained weights and training low-rank adapter matrices. Subsequent variants extend this approach through adaptive rank allocation across weight matrices ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , periodic merging of low-rank updates into the base weights ( Lialin et al., 2024 ) , and quantization of the frozen weights ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) .

Matrix-aware optimization exploits the structure of model parameters. Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) maintains factored preconditioners along individual dimensions. Xie et al. (2025) and An et al. (2025) further construct adaptive preconditioners from structured matrix gradients. A separate line of work focuses on reducing the memory cost of Muon. SUMO ( Refael et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the momentum within a dynamically adapted low-dimensional subspace, but its convergence guarantee is established only for reversible layers. LiMuon ( Huang et al., 2026 ) combines momentum-based variance reduction with randomized SVD to compress the stored gradient estimate, reducing the memory required for optimizer states. Gupta et al. (2025) reduce the memory cost of Muon through blockwise 8-bit quantization, while Su et al. (2026) further compress the optimizer states to 4-bit precision.

chunks.text: We present a practical variant of Algorithm 4 with the following two modifications. First, although the residual correction is explicitly scaled by γ \gamma , a single global coefficient cannot consistently align its magnitude with the projected Muon direction across parameter blocks and optimization steps. In particular, during early training, the initial subspace may leave a relatively large fraction of the gradient in the orthogonal complement, causing γ ​ ∥ ( I − P k ​ P k ⊤ ) ​ G k , t ∥ F \gamma\lVert(I-P_{k}P_{k}^{\top})G_{k,t}\rVert_{F} to substantially exceed ∥ P k ​ Z k , t ∥ F \lVert P_{k}Z_{k,t}\rVert_{F} . We observed that this scale imbalance coincides with pronounced loss fluctuations during the early stage of training. We introduce a residual cap that bounds the residual correction with respect to the projected Muon direction, while preserving the original coefficient γ \gamma whenever the residual update is already below the prescribed threshold.
